    49	```powershell
    50	git --version
    51	gh --version
    52	gh auth status
    53	```
    54	
    55	Also confirm Git's actual install layout — `CLAUDE.md` assumes the standard installer:
    56	
    57	```powershell
    58	Test-Path "C:\Program Files\Git\bin\bash.exe"
    59	Test-Path "C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\bash.exe"
    60	```
    61	
    62	Both should return `True`. The **first** path (`Git\bin\bash.exe`, ~45KB) is the MSYS2-env wrapper
    63	Claude Code needs to invoke. The second (`Git\usr\bin\bash.exe`, ~2.3MB) is the real bash binary —
    64	do **not** point config at that one; it's missing the MSYS2 env setup the wrapper provides.
    65	
    66	If either `Test-Path` returns `False`, find the real install root instead of guessing:
    67	
    68	```powershell
    69	(Get-Command git.exe).Source
    70	```
    71	
    72	This resolves to `<root>\cmd\git.exe` or `<root>\bin\git.exe` — strip to `<root>` and use
    73	`<root>\bin\bash.exe` as the wrapper path in Step 2.
    74	
    75	Confirm PATH does *not* silently resolve `bash` to the WSL launcher stub:
    76	
    77	```powershell
    78	where.exe bash
    79	```
    80	
    81	If this prints `...\AppData\Local\Microsoft\WindowsApps\bash.exe`, that's the WSL trap described in
    82	`CLAUDE.md` — note it in the report, but it doesn't block this runbook since we pin `shell: bash`
    83	plus `CLAUDE_CODE_GIT_BASH_PATH` explicitly (next step) rather than relying on bare `bash` on PATH.
    84	
    85	---
    86	
    87	## 2. Set required settings.json keys
    88	
    89	Locate the user-level Claude Code `settings.json` (ask the agent to find it via `claude config` /
    90	its own docs if the path isn't already known — do not guess a path). Add or confirm:
    91	
    92	```json
    93	{
    94	  "env": {
    95	    "CLAUDE_CODE_GIT_BASH_PATH": "C:\\Program Files\\Git\\bin\\bash.exe",
    96	    "CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_PREFER_HTTPS": "1"
    97	  }
    98	}
    99	```
   100	
   101	Adjust the path only if Step 1 showed Git installed somewhere non-standard. Preserve any existing
   102	keys already in the file — merge, don't overwrite.
   103

   105	session start; a session already running when the file was edited will not pick up the new values,
   106	which would make Step 3 fail in a way that looks like a plugin bug but isn't.
   107	
   108	---
   109	
   110	## 3. Install the plugin (marketplace path)
   111	
   112	```
   113	/plugin marketplace add Jointly-Shop/Petes-Pipeline
   114	/plugin install petes-pipeline@petes-pipeline
   115	```
   116

   118	install use `gh`'s HTTPS token instead of defaulting to SSH (which Pete's machine likely has no key
   119	for). If this step fails on auth, check `gh auth status` from Step 1 first before treating it as a
   120	plugin bug.
   121	
   122	Record: did it succeed, and if not, the exact error.
   123	
   124	---
   125	
   126	## 4. The core question: does the hook actually fire correctly on Windows
   127	
   128	Create an **isolated scratch git repo** (not this repo, not a Jointly-Shop project — a throwaway).
   129	Do **not** put it under `$env:TEMP`: Git for Windows typically mounts MSYS `/tmp` onto the same path
   130	as `%TEMP%`, and `detect-repo-state.sh` unconditionally `SKIP`s anything it resolves under `$TMPDIR`/
   131	`/tmp` — so a temp-dir scratch repo would silently fail the whole test regardless of the hooks
   132	actually working. Use somewhere under the user profile instead:
   133	
   134	```powershell
   135	$scratch = "$env:USERPROFILE\pilot-hook-test"
   136	$marker  = "$scratch\.pilot-hook-test-marker"
   137	if (Test-Path $scratch) {
   138	  if (Test-Path $marker) {
   139	    Remove-Item -Recurse -Force $scratch
   140	  } else {
   141	    Write-Host "STOP: $scratch already exists and has no marker from a prior run of this runbook. Do not delete it — it may be unrelated. Pick a different scratch path, or ask Mark."
   142	    # abort here — do not proceed to New-Item below
   143	  }
   144	}
   145	New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $scratch | Out-Null
   146	New-Item -ItemType File -Path $marker | Out-Null
   147	cd $scratch
   148	git init
   149	```
   150	
   151	The marker check is why it's safe to reuse this fixed path across reruns: `Remove-Item` only ever
   152	fires on a directory this runbook created itself (marker present), never on a same-named folder that
   153	happens to already exist for an unrelated reason. Reuse also matters beyond convenience — if a prior
   154	pass already ran `--decline` here, the leftover `.pilot/repo-offer.json` sentinel makes
   155	`detect-repo-state.sh` return `SKIP` on every later run too (sentinel check wins before anything else
   156	in the detector), which would silently mask a real hook failure as "offer correctly didn't show."
   157	
   158	With the plugin installed, start a Claude Code session in this scratch dir and run:
   159	
   160	```
   161	claude --debug hooks
   162	```

   165	different code path and gives a false green.
   166

   168	(`startup|resume|clear|compact`) and `session-start.sh` (`startup|clear`) share the `startup`
   169	trigger, so don't expect the new-project offer to show up later or separately; look for it in this
   170	same `--debug hooks` run / same session.
   171	
   172	**What to check, specifically:**
   173	
   174	1. Does the `operator-register.sh` hook actually invoke, or does it error before running?
   175	2. If it errors, is the error a path-resolution error (i.e. does the backslashed
   176	   `C:\Users\...\petes-pipeline\hooks\operator-register.sh` style path — substituted from
   177	   `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` — fail when handed to the MSYS `sh` invoked via the wrapper)? This is the
   178	   exact open question in `CLAUDE.md`'s Windows section — several upstream issues report backslash
   179	   paths failing as arguments to MSYS `sh`, including in quoted form, but it's undocumented and
   180	   unverified on a real box until now.
   181	3. Does the register content (plain-language operator preamble) actually appear injected into the
   182	   session context? (Ask the agent in-session something like "what operator register do you have
   183	   loaded" and see if it echoes the pete-safe register content.)
   184	4. Does `session-start.sh` also fire without error, and does it present the new-project offer (this
   185	   scratch dir is a fresh, unmanaged repo with no GitHub remote — it should qualify)?
   186	
   187	Record the raw `--debug hooks` output for both hook entries, not a summary.
   188	
   189	**Decline the offer.** The correct decline path is documented in `new-project-offer.md` and is safe
   190	to run for real: `sh '<plugin-hooks-path>/repo-offer-apply.sh' --decline .` — the agent should invoke
   191	this itself when you say no, exactly as it would for Pete. It writes a `.pilot/repo-offer.json`
   192	sentinel in the scratch repo (expected) and suppresses re-offering; confirm `git remote -v` shows no
   193	new remote and nothing was pushed. Do **not** let the agent choose the yes path (`--publish` /
   194	`--local-only`).
   195	
   196	---
   197	
   198	## Report
   199	
   200	Fill in and return this section:
   201	
   202	| Check | Result | Notes / raw error |
   203	|---|---|---|
   204	| `git --version` / `gh --version` / `gh auth status` | | |
   205	| Git bash paths present at expected locations | | |
   206	| `where.exe bash` resolves to (WSL stub? real path?) | | |
   207	| settings.json `env` keys set | | |

   210	| **Backslash `C:\…` path survives as arg to MSYS `sh`?** | yes/no | this is the headline finding |
   211	| Operator register content visibly injected | pass/fail | |
   212	| `session-start.sh` hook fires without error | pass/fail | |
   213	| New-project offer renders correctly | pass/fail | |
   214	| Decline path runs cleanly (sentinel written, no remote/push) | pass/fail | |
   215	
   216	**If the backslash-path check fails:** stop here and report back rather than attempting a fix. The
   217	fix (if needed) is a repo change (e.g. rewriting the affected hooks in Node, per `CLAUDE.md`'s note

### README.md
# Pete's Pipeline

A Claude Code **plugin**: a guided `/build` pipeline for non-technical operators. A request goes
in; the pipeline classifies its effect, implements it, reviews and verifies it, and either
self-publishes safe changes or holds dangerous/irreversible ones for the maintainer. The real
safety boundary is server-side (GitHub branch protection + CODEOWNERS + required checks); the
client-side skill is advisory judgment and UX.

**Status:** transition in progress. The prereq layer (harness contract + ledger validator +
red-glob machinery), the per-project profile spec + reusable red-glob-drift CI action, and
new-project detection (SessionStart offer + consent-gated apply-script) are in place and tested.
The orchestrator (`skills/build/SKILL.md`) is a stub until assembly step A1.

## Layout

```
.claude-plugin/        plugin.json + self-hosted marketplace.json
skills/build/
  SKILL.md             orchestrator (stub; assembled at A1)
  HARNESS.md           S0 contract — vocabulary, interfaces, fixture protocol
  lib/
    ledger-validate.php  S1 Evidence-Receipt ledger validator
    gen-codeowners.sh    fail-closed CODEOWNERS generator from a red-glob manifest
  tests/                 ledger validator + portable red-glob drift machinery + self-test
skills/explain/        plain-language operator help (read-only; explains and hands back)
.github/actions/red-glob-drift/  reusable composite action targets reference in their CI
hooks/                 new-project detection: SessionStart offers backup for an unmanaged project
                       (read-only detector -> plain-language offer -> consent-gated apply-script)
docs/
  profile-spec.md        the .pilot/ schema each target repo supplies
  TRANSITION-PLAN.md     the multi-phase extraction roadmap
```

## Design separation

- **Portable core (this repo):** project-agnostic skills, machinery, and hooks.
- **Per-project profile (`.pilot/` in each target repo):** red-path manifest, deploy adapter,
  enforcement level, operator register.
- **Per-machine activation:** the plugin is *enabled* only on operator machines. Maintainers who
  merely hold the repo are never activated.

## Tests

```sh
sh skills/build/tests/ledger-validate.test.sh          # S1 ledger validator
sh skills/build/tests/red-globs-drift.selftest.sh      # portable drift machinery
sh .github/actions/red-glob-drift/bind-and-run.test.sh # CI action binding (authoritative + fail-closed)
sh hooks/tests/detect-repo-state.test.sh               # new-project detector state table
sh hooks/tests/operator-register.test.sh               # operator register resolution (tone)
sh hooks/tests/session-start.test.sh                   # SessionStart offer wrapper
sh hooks/tests/repo-offer-apply.test.sh                # consent-gated apply-script invariants
```

Run every `.sh` under both `dash` and `bash`.

L752:   * cite301†CLI customization L753:   * cite302†Developer commands L754:   * cite303†Developer settings L755: # Hooks
L756: 
L757: Run deterministic scripts during the Codex lifecycle
L758: 
L759: Copy Page
L760: 
L761: Hooks are an extensibility framework for Codex. They allow you to inject your own scripts into the agentic loop, enabling features such as:
L762:   * Send the chat to a custom logging/analytics engine
L763:   * Scan your team’s prompts to block accidentally pasting API keys
L764:   * Summarize chats to create persistent memories automatically
L765:   * Run a custom validation check when a chat turn stops, enforcing standards
L766:   * Customize prompting when in a certain directory
L767: 
L768: Runtime behavior to keep in mind:
L769:   * Matching hooks from multiple files all run.
L770:   * Multiple matching command hooks for the same event are launched concurrently, so one hook can’t prevent another matching hook from starting.
L771:   * Non-managed command hooks must be reviewed and trusted before they run.
L772: 
L773: Hooks run at different points in a conversation:
L774: When  | Hooks
L775: --- | ---
L776: During a turn  | `PreToolUse`, `PermissionRequest`, `PostToolUse`, `PreCompact`, `PostCompact`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SubagentStop`, `Stop`
L777: When a session or subagent starts  | `SessionStart`, `SubagentStart`
L778: When the main thread ends  | `SessionEnd` (doesn’t run for subagents)
L779: ## Where Codex looks for hooks
L780: 
L781: Codex discovers hooks next to active config layers in either of these forms:
L782: 
L783:   * `hooks.json`
L784:   * inline `[hooks]` tables inside `config.toml`
L785: 
L786: Installed plugins can also bundle lifecycle config through their plugin manifest or a default `hooks/hooks.json` file. See cite414†Build plugins†developers.openai.com for the plugin packaging rules.
L787: 
L788: In practice, the four most useful locations are:
L789:   * `~/.codex/hooks.json`
L790:   * `~/.codex/config.toml`
L791:   * `<repo>/.codex/hooks.json`
L792:   * `<repo>/.codex/config.toml`
L793: 
L794: If more than one hook source exists, Codex loads all matching hooks. Higher-precedence config layers don’t replace lower-precedence hooks. If a single layer contains both `hooks.json` and inline `[hooks]`, Codex merges them and warns at startup. Prefer one representation per layer.
L795: Codex can also discover hooks bundled with enabled plugins. Plugin-bundled hooks load alongside other hook sources and use the same trust-review flow as other non-managed hooks.
L796: 
L797: Project-local hooks load only when the project `.codex/` layer is trusted. In untrusted projects, Codex still loads user and system hooks from their own active config layers.
L798: ## Review and trust hooks
L799: 
L800: Codex lists configured hooks before deciding which ones can run. Before a non-managed command hook can run, Codex requires you to review and trust the exact hook definition. Codex records trust against the hook’s current hash, so new or changed hooks are marked for review and skipped until trusted.
L801: Use `/hooks` in the CLI to inspect hook sources, review new or changed hooks, trust hooks, or disable individual non-managed hooks. If hooks need review at startup, Codex prints a warning that tells you to open `/hooks`.
L802: 
L803: Managed hooks from system, MDM, cloud, or `requirements.toml` sources are marked as managed, trusted by policy, and can’t be disabled from the user hook browser.
L804: For one-off automation that already vets hook sources outside Codex, pass `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` to run enabled hooks without requiring persisted hook trust for that invocation.
L805: ## Config shape
L806: 
L807: Hooks are organized in three levels:
L808:   * A hook event such as `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PreCompact`, `SubagentStart`, or `Stop`
L809:   * A matcher group that decides when that event matches

L1086: ## Hooks
L1087: ### SessionStart
L1088: 
L1089: `matcher` is applied to `source` for this event.
L1090: 
L1091: Fields in addition to cite418†Common input fields :
L1092: 
L1093: Field  | Type  | Meaning
L1094: --- | --- | ---
L1095: `source`  | `string`  | How the session started: `startup`, `resume`, `clear`, or `compact`
L1096: 
L1097: Plain text on `stdout` is added as extra developer context.
L1098: JSON on `stdout` supports cite419†Common output fields and this hook-specific shape:
L1099: 
L1100:     `{
L1101:       "hookSpecificOutput": {
L1102:         "hookEventName": "SessionStart",
L1103:         "additionalContext": "Load the workspace conventions before editing."
L1104:       }
L1105:     }`
L1106: 
L1107: That `additionalContext` text is added as extra developer context.
L1108: After Codex compacts a root session, `SessionStart` hooks that match `source: "compact"` run before the next model request. This also applies when automatic compaction happens in the middle of a turn: Codex delivers the hook’s additional context to the immediate continuation instead of waiting for a later user turn. If the hook returns `continue: false`, Codex ends the turn without sending another model request.
L1109: ### SessionEnd
L1110: 
L1111: `SessionEnd` lets you run a command when a session ends, such as saving final notes or cleaning up files. It runs for the main thread when you archive or delete a conversation that’s still open, when Codex closes normally, or after a conversation has been idle and isn’t open in any connected client for 30 minutes. It won’t run for subagents.
L1112: Switching away from a conversation or calling `thread/unsubscribe` doesn’t end the session right away, so it won’t immediately run `SessionEnd`. Your hook can still read the session transcript while it runs.
L1113: 
L1114: `matcher` filters `reason` for this event. For now, `reason` is always `other`. You can omit `matcher` or use `other` to run on every `SessionEnd` event.

L1283: #### Tool calls from code mode
L1284: 
L1285: When a model uses code mode to call a tool from JavaScript, hook decisions apply to that nested call. `PreToolUse` can stop the tool before it runs or rewrite its input. A blocking `PostToolUse` can’t undo the tool’s side effects, but it can keep the original result from reaching the running script.

L1288: `PreToolUse` blocks  | The tool promise rejects before the tool runs.
L1289: `PreToolUse` returns `updatedInput`  | The tool runs with the rewritten input and the promise resolves with that result.
L1290: `PostToolUse` returns `decision: "block"` or exits with code `2`  | The tool runs, then the promise rejects with the hook reason.
L1291: `PostToolUse` returns `continue: false`  | Codex uses the hook feedback for the model-visible result, but doesn’t reject the nested tool promise.

L937: ## Turn hooks off
L938: 
L939: Hooks are enabled by default. To turn them off in `config.toml`, set:
L940: 
L941:     `[features]
L942:     hooks = false`
L943: 
L944: Use `hooks` as the canonical feature key. `codex_hooks` still works as a deprecated alias. Admins can force hooks off the same way in `requirements.toml` with `[features].hooks = false`.
L945: ## Managed hooks from `requirements.toml`
L946: Enterprise-managed requirements can also define hooks inline under `[hooks]`. This is useful when admins want to enforce the hook configuration while delivering the actual scripts through MDM or another device-management system. To enforce managed hooks even for users who disabled hooks locally, pin `[features].hooks = true` in `requirements.toml` alongside `[hooks]`. To ignore user, project, session, and plugin hooks while still allowing administrator managed hooks, set `allow_managed_hooks_only = true`.
L947: 
L948:     `allow_managed_hooks_only = true
L949: 
L950:     [features]
L951:     hooks = true
L952: 
L953:     [hooks]
L954:     managed_dir = "/enterprise/hooks"
L955:     windows_managed_dir = 'C:\enterprise\hooks'
L956: 
L957:     [[hooks.PreToolUse]]
L958:     matcher = "^Bash$"
L959: 
L960:     [[hooks.PreToolUse.hooks]]
L961:     type = "command"
L962:     command = "python3 /enterprise/hooks/pre_tool_use_policy.py"
L963:     command_windows = 'py -3 C:\enterprise\hooks\pre_tool_use_policy.py'
L964:     timeout = 30
L965:     statusMessage = "Checking managed Bash command"`
L966: Notes for managed hooks:
L967:   * `managed_dir` is used on macOS and Linux.
L968:   * `windows_managed_dir` is used on Windows.
L969:   * Codex doesn’t distribute the scripts in `managed_dir`; your enterprise tooling must install and update them separately.
L970:   * Managed hook commands should use absolute script paths under the configured managed directory.
L971:   * `allow_managed_hooks_only = true` skips hooks from user, project, session, and plugin sources, but still loads managed hooks from `requirements.toml` and other managed config layers.
L972: ## Plugin-bundled hooks
L973: 
L974: When a plugin is enabled, Codex can load lifecycle hooks from that plugin alongside user, project, and managed hooks.
L975: By default, Codex looks for `hooks/hooks.json` inside the plugin root. A plugin manifest can override that default with a `hooks` entry in `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`. The manifest entry can be a `./`-prefixed path, an array of `./`-prefixed paths, an inline hooks object, or an array of inline hooks objects.
L976: 
L977:     `{
L978:       "name": "repo-policy",
L979:       "hooks": "./hooks/hooks.json"
L980:     }`
L981: Manifest hook paths are resolved relative to the plugin root and must stay inside that root. If a manifest defines `hooks`, Codex uses those manifest entries instead of the default `hooks/hooks.json`.
L982: 
L983: Plugin hook commands receive these environment variables:
L984:   * `PLUGIN_ROOT` is a Codex-specific extension that points to the installed plugin root.
L985:   * `PLUGIN_DATA` is a Codex-specific extension that points to the plugin’s writable data directory.
L986:   * Codex also sets `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` and `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA` for compatibility with existing plugin hooks.
L987: Plugin hooks use the same event schema as other hooks. Installing or enabling a plugin doesn’t automatically trust its hooks; Codex skips plugin-bundled hooks until you review and trust the current hook definition.

L990: The `matcher` field is a regex string that filters when hooks fire. Use `"*"`, `""`, or omit `matcher` entirely to match every occurrence of a supported event.
L991: 
L992: Only some current Codex events honor `matcher`:
L993: Event  | What `matcher` filters  | Notes
L994: --- | --- | ---
L995: `PermissionRequest`  | tool name  | Support includes `Bash`, `apply_patch`*, and MCP tool names
L996: `PostToolUse`  | tool name  | See cite416†Tool coverage L997: `PostCompact`  | compaction trigger  | Values are `manual` or `auto`
L998: `PreCompact`  | compaction trigger  | Values are `manual` or `auto`
L999: `PreToolUse`  | tool name  | See cite416†Tool coverage L1000: `SessionEnd`  | end reason  | Currently only `other`
L1001: `SessionStart`  | start source  | Values are `startup`, `resume`, `clear`, and `compact`
L1002: `SubagentStart`  | subagent type  | Values depend on the subagent that starts
L1003: `SubagentStop`  | subagent type  | Values depend on the subagent that stops
L1004: `UserPromptSubmit`  | not supported  | Any configured `matcher` is ignored for this event
L1005: `Stop`  | not supported  | Any configured `matcher` is ignored for this event
L1006: *For `apply_patch`, `matcher` values can also use `Edit` or `Write`.

L1008: Examples:
L1009: 
L1010:   * `Bash`
L1011:   * `^apply_patch$`
L1012:   * `Edit|Write`
L1013:   * `mcp__filesystem__read_file`
L1014:   * `mcp__filesystem__.*`
L1015:   * `startup|resume|clear|compact`
L1016:   * `manual|auto`
L1017: ### Tool coverage
L1018: 
L1019: `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` can observe more than shell and MCP calls. Most local function tools use the same hook path, so you can match their tool name, inspect their JSON arguments, and, for `PreToolUse`, block or rewrite the call.
L1020: Tool path  | `PreToolUse`  | `PostToolUse`  | Notes
L1021: --- | --- | --- | ---
L1022: Shell commands  | Yes  | Yes  | Match as `Bash`.
L1023: Unified exec (`exec_command`)  | Yes  | Yes  | Match as `Bash`. A later `write_stdin` poll can deliver the original command’s `PostToolUse` when that command finishes.
L1024: `apply_patch`  | Yes  | Yes  | Match as `apply_patch`, `Edit`, or `Write`.
L1025: MCP tools  | Yes  | Yes  | Match the MCP tool name, such as `mcp__filesystem__read_file`.
L1026: Other local function tools  | Yes  | Yes  | Match the function tool name, such as `update_plan`. `spawn_agent` also matches `Agent`.
L1027: Hosted tools, such as `WebSearch`  | No  | No  | These don’t use the local function-tool hook path.
L1028: `write_stdin` is transport for an existing unified-exec session. It doesn’t run `PreToolUse` again when it sends input or polls a command that already passed `PreToolUse`.
L1029: 
L1030: Some specialized tool paths can opt out of the default hook path. Treat tool hooks as a useful guardrail, not a complete enforcement boundary.

+#!/usr/bin/env bash
+set -euo pipefail
+
+# Heredocs are banned from the hook delivery chain: bash >= 5.1 delivers
+# them through a pre-fork pipe write that deadlocks on macOS under pipe
+# pressure (issue #571; the #571 class). This fence fails the moment one
+# returns. The operator is spelled out of a variable so this file does not
+# trip its own check.
+SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)"
+REPO_ROOT="$(cd "$SCRIPT_DIR/../.." && pwd)"
+
+OP='<''<'
+FAILURES=0
+for f in "$REPO_ROOT"/hooks/*; do
+    case "$f" in *.json) continue;; esac
+    [ -f "$f" ] || continue
+    if hits="$(grep -nE "$OP" "$f")"; then
+        echo "  [FAIL] heredoc operator in ${f#"$REPO_ROOT"/}:"
+        printf '%s\n' "$hits" | sed 's/^/    /'
+        FAILURES=$((FAILURES + 1))
+    else

 # Cross-Platform Polyglot Hooks for Claude Code
 
 Claude Code plugins need hooks that work on Windows, macOS, and Linux. This document describes the single generic dispatcher pattern used in `hooks/run-hook.cmd`.
 
 > **Authoritative source:** `hooks/run-hook.cmd` is the canonical implementation. When this document and the code diverge, trust the code.
 
 ## The Problem
 
 Claude Code runs hook commands through a shell:
 - **macOS/Linux**: bash or sh
 - **Windows with Git Bash installed**: Git Bash
 - **Windows without Git Bash**: PowerShell (older versions used CMD.exe)
 
 Neither Windows fallback shell can parse our command string: PowerShell treats
 a leading quoted path as a string expression and errors on the next bareword,
 and CMD.exe's `/c` quoting rules strip the outer quotes when the path contains
 a metacharacter such as `(`. Our hooks therefore declare `"shell": "bash"`
 (supported since Claude Code 2.1.81; older versions ignore the key), which
 forces the Git Bash route and, when Git Bash is absent, produces an actionable
 "install Git for Windows" error instead of a shell parser failure.
 
 This creates several challenges:
 
 1. **Script execution**: Windows CMD can't execute `.sh` files directly
 2. **Path format**: Windows uses backslashes (`C:\path`), Unix uses forward slashes (`/path`)
 3. **Environment variables**: `$VAR` syntax doesn't work in CMD
 4. **`.sh` auto-prepend**: Claude Code on Windows automatically prepends `bash` to any command that contains `.sh` in its path — this interferes with the dispatcher if scripts have extensions
 
 ## The Solution: Extensionless Scripts + Single Generic Dispatcher
 
 The repo uses one generic `run-hook.cmd` dispatcher for all hooks. Hook scripts are **extensionless** (`session-start`, not `session-start.sh`). This is deliberate: it prevents Claude Code's Windows auto-detection from prepending `bash` to the dispatcher command and breaking it.
 
 ### File Structure
 
 ```
 hooks/
 ├── hooks.json          # Points to run-hook.cmd with extensionless script name
 ├── run-hook.cmd        # Cross-platform dispatcher (the polyglot wrapper)
 └── session-start       # Actual hook logic — extensionless bash script
 ```
 
 ### hooks.json
 
 ```json
 {
   "hooks": {
     "SessionStart": [
       {
         "matcher": "startup|clear|compact",
         "hooks": [
           {
             "type": "command",
             "command": "\"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/run-hook.cmd\" session-start",
             "shell": "bash",
             "async": false
           }
         ]
       }
     ]
   }
 }
 ```
 
 The path is quoted because `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` may contain spaces.
 
 ## How `run-hook.cmd` Works at a High Level
 
-`run-hook.cmd` is a polyglot script: Windows treats the first block as batch
-commands, while Unix shells treat that block as a no-op heredoc and continue
-after it.
+`run-hook.cmd` is a polyglot script: its first lines start with `:;`, which
+cmd.exe skips as labels and Unix shells execute — the shell execs the hook
+before ever reaching the batch block that Windows runs.
 
 Do not copy an implementation from this document. Read `hooks/run-hook.cmd`
 directly when changing the dispatcher, and run `tests/hooks/test-session-start.sh`
 afterward.
 
 ### How it works on Windows (CMD.exe)
 
 1. The batch section validates the script name and resolves the hook directory
    from the dispatcher's own location.
 2. It tries bash in three places:
    - `C:\Program Files\Git\bin\bash.exe`
    - `C:\Program Files (x86)\Git\bin\bash.exe`
    - `bash` on `PATH` (MSYS2, Cygwin, or a non-default Git install)
 3. If bash is found, it runs the named extensionless hook script from the hooks
    directory.
 4. If no bash is found, the dispatcher exits `0` silently — the plugin
    continues working, it just skips the hook.
 5. `exit /b` stops CMD before it reaches the Unix section.
 
 ### How it works on Unix (bash/sh)
 
-1. `: << 'CMDBLOCK'` opens a heredoc on a no-op command.
-2. The entire CMD batch block is consumed by the heredoc and ignored.
-3. After `CMDBLOCK`, bash resolves the script directory and `exec`s the named
-   extensionless script directly.
+1. Each leading `:;` line is a no-op label to cmd.exe but real commands to a
+   POSIX shell.
+2. The shell checks bash exists (silent exit 0 if not), resolves the script
+   directory CDPATH-proof, and `exec`s the named extensionless script — it
+   never reads the batch block at all.
+3. Heredocs are banned in this file and all hooks/ executables (issue #571:
+   bash >= 5.1 pre-fork pipe writes deadlock on macOS under pipe pressure);
+   `tests/hooks/test-no-heredocs-in-hooks.sh` enforces the ban.
 
 ### Key design decisions
 
 | Decision | Why |
 |----------|-----|
 | Extensionless scripts | Prevents Claude Code's Windows `.sh`-auto-prepend from interfering with the dispatcher command |
 | No `-l` (login shell) | Not needed; hook scripts should be self-contained and not depend on login-shell PATH setup |
 | No `cygpath` | Bash receives the Windows path directly and handles it correctly; `cygpath` was needed by the old `-c "..."` invocation pattern, not by direct exec |
 | Silent exit on no-bash | Avoids breaking the plugin for users who don't have Git for Windows; hook context injection is skipped gracefully |
 
 ## Writing Cross-Platform Hook Scripts
 
 Your hook logic goes in the extensionless script file. A few portable patterns:
 
 ### Do
 - Use pure bash builtins when possible
 - Use `$(command)` instead of backticks
 - Quote all variable expansions: `"$VAR"`
 
 ### Avoid
 - Relying on PATH-dependent tools without fallbacks (the hook runs without `-l`, so login-shell PATH is not set)
 - Giving scripts a `.sh` extension — this triggers Claude Code's Windows auto-prepend
 
 ### Example: JSON escaping without external tools
 
 ```bash
 escape_for_json() {
     local input="$1"
     local output=""
     local i char
     for (( i=0; i<${#input}; i++ )); do
         char="${input:$i:1}"
         case "$char" in
             $'\\') output+='\\' ;;
             '"') output+='\"' ;;
             $'\n') output+='\n' ;;
             $'\r') output+='\r' ;;
             $'\t') output+='\t' ;;
             *) output+="$char" ;;
         esac
     done
     printf '%s' "$output"
 }
 ```
 
 ## Troubleshooting
 
 ### "bash is not recognized"
 
 CMD couldn't find bash in any of the three locations the dispatcher tries. The dispatcher exits silently (0) rather than erroring, so the hook is skipped. Install Git for Windows at the standard path or ensure `bash` is on `PATH`.
 
 ### Hook runs on Unix but does nothing on Windows
 
 Check that the script filename is **extensionless** in `hooks.json`. A command like `run-hook.cmd session-start.sh` can trigger Claude Code's `.sh` auto-detection and bypass the intended CMD dispatcher path, or just try to run a non-existent `session-start.sh` script.
 
 ### Hook doesn't fire at all
 
 Verify the `matcher` in `hooks.json` matches the event type your harness emits. Claude Code uses `startup|clear|compact`; Cursor uses `sessionStart`. Check `hooks-cursor.json` for the Cursor variant.
 
 ## Related Issues
 
 - [anthropics/claude-code#9758](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/9758) — `.sh` scripts open in editor on Windows
 - [anthropics/claude-code#3417](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/3417) — Hooks don't work on Windows

L1018: 
L1019: `PreToolUse` and `PostToolUse` can observe more than shell and MCP calls. Most local function tools use the same hook path, so you can match their tool name, inspect their JSON arguments, and, for `PreToolUse`, block or rewrite the call.
L1020: Tool path  | `PreToolUse`  | `PostToolUse`  | Notes
L1021: --- | --- | --- | ---
L1022: Shell commands  | Yes  | Yes  | Match as `Bash`.
L1023: Unified exec (`exec_command`)  | Yes  | Yes  | Match as `Bash`. A later `write_stdin` poll can deliver the original command’s `PostToolUse` when that command finishes.
L1024: `apply_patch`  | Yes  | Yes  | Match as `apply_patch`, `Edit`, or `Write`.
L1025: MCP tools  | Yes  | Yes  | Match the MCP tool name, such as `mcp__filesystem__read_file`.
L1026: Other local function tools  | Yes  | Yes  | Match the function tool name, such as `update_plan`. `spawn_agent` also matches `Agent`.
L1027: Hosted tools, such as `WebSearch`  | No  | No  | These don’t use the local function-tool hook path.

L1210: ### PermissionRequest
L1211: 
L1212: `PermissionRequest` runs when Codex is about to ask for approval, such as a shell escalation or managed-network approval. It can allow the request, deny the request, or decline to decide and let the normal approval prompt continue. It doesn’t run for commands that don’t need approval.

L795: Codex can also discover hooks bundled with enabled plugins. Plugin-bundled hooks load alongside other hook sources and use the same trust-review flow as other non-managed hooks.
L796: 
L797: Project-local hooks load only when the project `.codex/` layer is trusted. In untrusted projects, Codex still loads user and system hooks from their own active config layers.
L798: ## Review and trust hooks
L799: 
L800: Codex lists configured hooks before deciding which ones can run. Before a non-managed command hook can run, Codex requires you to review and trust the exact hook definition. Codex records trust against the hook’s current hash, so new or changed hooks are marked for review and skipped until trusted.
L801: Use `/hooks` in the CLI to inspect hook sources, review new or changed hooks, trust hooks, or disable individual non-managed hooks. If hooks need review at startup, Codex prints a warning that tells you to open `/hooks`.
L802: 
L803: Managed hooks from system, MDM, cloud, or `requirements.toml` sources are marked as managed, trusted by policy, and can’t be disabled from the user hook browser.
L804: For one-off automation that already vets hook sources outside Codex, pass `--dangerously-bypass-hook-trust` to run enabled hooks without requiring persisted hook trust for that invocation.
L808:   * A hook event such as `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PreCompact`, `SubagentStart`, or `Stop`
L809:   * A matcher group that decides when that event matches
L810:   * One or more hook handlers that run when the matcher group matches
L811: 
L812:     `{
L813:       "description": "Optional lifecycle hooks for this workspace.",
L814:       "hooks": {
L815:         "SessionStart": [
L816:           {
L817:             "matcher": "startup|resume",
L818:             "hooks": [
L819:               {
L820:                 "type": "command",
L889:                 "type": "command",
L890:                 "command": "/usr/bin/python3 \"$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.codex/hooks/stop_continue.py\"",
L891:                 "timeout": 30
L892:               }
L893:             ]
L894:           }
L895:         ]
L896:       }
L897:     }`
L898: Notes:
L899:   * `description` is optional top-level metadata for a `hooks.json` file. It doesn’t change which hooks run.
L900:   * `timeout` is in seconds.
L901:   * If `timeout` is omitted, Codex uses `600` seconds for most hooks.
L902:     * `SessionEnd` uses `1` second by default and supports up to `3` seconds.
L903:   * `statusMessage` is optional.
L904:   * `additionalContextLimit` sets how much `additionalContext` a command hook can send to the model before Codex saves the full text to disk and sends a shorter preview instead. See cite415†Large hook output .
L905:   * `commandWindows` is an optional Windows-only command override. In TOML, use `command_windows` or `commandWindows`.
L906:   * The `async` option is parsed, but asynchronous command hooks aren’t supported yet.
L907:   * Only `type: "command"` handlers run today. `prompt` and `agent` handlers are parsed but skipped.
L908:   * Commands run with the session `cwd` as their working directory.
L909:   * For repo-local hooks, prefer resolving from the git root instead of using a relative path such as `.codex/hooks/...`. Codex may be started from a subdirectory, and a git-root-based path keeps the hook location stable.

L1031: ## Common input fields
L1032:

L1034: 
L1035: These are the shared fields you will usually use:
L1036: Field  | Type  | Meaning
L1037: --- | --- | ---
L1038: `session_id`  | `string`  | Current Codex session id. Subagent hooks use the parent session id.
L1039: `transcript_path`  | `string | null`  | Path to the session transcript file, if any
L1040: `cwd`  | `string`  | Working directory for the session

L1046:

L1050: ## Common output fields
L1051: 
L1052: `SessionStart`, `PreCompact`, `PostCompact`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SubagentStop`, and `Stop` support these shared JSON fields. `SubagentStart` accepts the same shape for `systemMessage` and hook-specific context, but `continue: false` doesn’t stop the subagent:
L1053: 
L1054:     `{
L1055:       "continue": true,
L1056:       "stopReason": "optional",
L1057:       "systemMessage": "optional",
L1058:       "suppressOutput": false
L1059:     }`
L1060: Field  | Effect
L1061: --- | ---
L1062: `continue`  | If `false`, marks that hook run as stopped
L1063: `stopReason`  | Recorded as the reason for stopping
L1064: `systemMessage`  | Surfaced as a warning in the UI or event stream
L1065: `suppressOutput`  | Parsed today but not yet implemented
L1066: 
L1067: Exit `0` with no output is treated as success and Codex continues.
L1068: `PreToolUse` and `PermissionRequest` support `systemMessage`, but `continue`, `stopReason`, and `suppressOutput` aren’t currently supported for those events. If a `PreToolUse` hook returns one of those unsupported fields, Codex marks that hook run as failed, reports the error, and continues the tool call.
L1069: 
L1070: `PostToolUse` supports `systemMessage`, `continue: false`, and `stopReason`. `suppressOutput` is parsed but not currently supported for that event.
L1071: ### Large hook output
L1072: 
L1073: By default, Codex limits each model-visible hook-output message to roughly 2,500 tokens. If a hook returns more, Codex saves the full text under `<temp_dir>/hook_outputs/<session_id>/<uuid>.txt` and gives the model a head-and-tail preview with the saved-file path. This behavior is called spilling: Codex stores oversized output on disk and replaces it with a shorter, model-visible preview. If the file can’t be written, the model still receives a truncated preview.
L1074: Keep hook and plugin context concise. Context from multiple hooks and plugins adds up and can degrade model performance. Raising `additionalContextLimit` increases that risk. Avoid setting the limit to `0` unless the hook enforces a strict output cap; otherwise, a single hook can consume the entire context window.
L1075: For any command hook that returns `additionalContext`, set `additionalContextLimit` on the handler to customize the approximate token threshold:
L1076: 
L1077:     `{
L1078:       "type": "command",
L1079:       "command": "python3 ~/.codex/hooks/session_start.py",
L1080:       "additionalContextLimit": 5000
L1081:     }`
L1082: Omit `additionalContextLimit` to use the default `2500`-token threshold. Use a positive integer to select a different threshold, or `0` to pass the handler’s complete additional context directly to the model. Codex evaluates each matching handler independently. For events that can’t produce additional context, Codex ignores `additionalContextLimit` and reports a configuration warning.
L1083: 
L1084: The setting applies only to `additionalContext`. Tool feedback and continuation prompts keep the default limit.
L1085: Because oversized output can be written to disk, avoid returning secrets or other sensitive data in hook output.

L763: 
L764: Assemble skills and MCP server dependencies into a distributable plugin.
L765: 
L766: Copy Page
L767: 
L768: After building your cite164†skills and, when needed, an cite161†MCP server , assemble those parts into the plugin people will install. Packaging gives the plugin a stable identity and tells ChatGPT and Codex which skills, MCP server connections, and other resources belong together.
L769: Every plugin has a `.codex-plugin/plugin.json` manifest. Depending on the plugin’s architecture, its folder can also include:
L770: 
L771:   * A `skills/` directory containing the workflows you built.
L772:   * An `.app.json` file that references a registered MCP server connection. The filename is a compatibility identifier; the underlying primitive is the MCP server.
L773:   * An `.mcp.json` file for an MCP server distributed with the plugin.
L774:   * Optional assets and lifecycle hooks.
L775: UI and authentication remain part of the MCP server integration you built in the preceding steps; the plugin manifest connects that integration to the rest of the package.
L776: 
L777: Public plugins are published once to the universal plugin directory shared by ChatGPT and Codex. Local and repo marketplaces are separate authoring, testing, and team-distribution sources, and their availability can vary by surface.
L778: Use `@plugin-creator` for the fastest path, or create the manifest and folder structure manually. Both approaches produce the same plugin structure.
L779: 
L780: For complete public examples, inspect cite408†Figma†github.com , cite409†Notion†github.com , and cite410†Build web apps†github.com .
L781: ## Package with `@plugin-creator`
L782: 
L783: For the fastest setup, use the built-in `@plugin-creator` skill.
L784: 
L785: cite411†Image: Plugin creator skill in ChatGPT L786: 
L787: It scaffolds the required `.codex-plugin/plugin.json` manifest and can also generate a local marketplace entry for testing. If you already have a plugin folder, you can still use `@plugin-creator` to wire it into a local marketplace.
L788: 
L789: cite412†Image: how to invoke the plugin-creator skill L790: ### Create and test a plugin locally with an MCP server
L791: 
L792: You can also use the plugin-creator skill to test a plugin that includes an MCP server. The plugin still needs a local folder and manifest, and you first register the MCP server connection in ChatGPT developer mode.
L793: 
L794: First, enable developer mode in ChatGPT:
L795: 
L796:   1. Open cite407†ChatGPT†chatgpt.com .
L797:   2. Open Settings.
L798:   3. Select Security and login.
L799:   4. Turn on Developer mode.
L800: 
L801: Then register the MCP server in developer mode:
L802:   1. Go to cite413†ChatGPT Plugins†chatgpt.com .
L803:   2. Select the plus button.
L804:   3. Complete the modal with your MCP server URL and connection details.
L805:   4. After ChatGPT creates the connection, copy its technical ID from the browser URL. It starts with `plugin_asdk_app`.
L806: 
L807: Give that `plugin_asdk_app...` ID to `@plugin-creator` in Work mode in ChatGPT or `$plugin-creator` in Codex. For example, in Work mode:
L808: 
L809: Plugin Creator prompt
L810: `@plugin-creator create a plugin for ChatGPT and Codex using my MCP server. Use plugin_asdk_app_6a4c0062f3b88191855c0a80eac5d53d and name it Acme Support. Include a personal marketplace entry so I can test it locally.`
L811: 
L812: The plugin-creator skill will create the plugin folder, create the required `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, and add MCP server wiring for the plugin. If you ask it to create a personal marketplace entry, the plugin appears under your local source in the Plugins Directory for testing.

   743	## Part 7 — Cross-platform / Windows
   744	
   745	Only relevant to the shell-hook shape. `hooks/run-hook.cmd` is a polyglot: a
   746	single file that's valid as both a Windows batch script and a Unix shell script.
   747	On Windows, `cmd.exe` runs the batch portion, which locates `bash` (Git for
   748	Windows, then `bash` on PATH) and runs the named hook script; if no bash is
   749	found it exits cleanly so the harness still works, just without injection. On
   750	Unix, the leading `:` makes the batch block a no-op and the shell runs the
   751	script directly.
   752	
   753	Two rules this enforces, which you must respect:
   754	
   755	- **Hook scripts are extensionless** (`session-start`, not `session-start.sh`).
   756	  Claude Code's Windows handling prepends `bash` to any command containing
   757	  `.sh`, which would double-invoke. Name your hook script without an extension.
   758	- Don't write per-OS variants of the hook script. One extensionless bash script
   759	  plus the polyglot wrapper covers all three platforms.
   760	
   761	`hooks/run-hook.cmd` itself is the authoritative implementation — read it. See

   801	  to get Superpowers, the acceptance test fails. Re-read Part 2.

### HIGH — Codex compaction hook can deadlock before reaching its script

**File:** `hooks/hooks-codex.json:9`

**Evidence:** The new production command dispatches through `hooks/run-hook.cmd`, but at this commit that wrapper starts with a 1.4 KB `: << 'CMDBLOCK'` heredoc. On macOS with Bash ≥5.1 under pipe pressure, the heredoc is written to a small pre-fork pipe and can deadlock, causing the 30-second hook timeout and preventing the post-compaction bootstrap from being restored. Repository branches from the same base contain the confirming RED test (`431915a`) and heredoc-free fix (`d80fc18`, issue #571). The new test bypasses the production path at `tests/hooks/test-session-start-codex.sh:23` by invoking `session-start-codex` directly, so it cannot expose this failure.

**Suggested fix:** Rebase/merge the heredoc-free `run-hook.cmd` implementation before shipping, and change the Codex test to invoke the configured wrapper (`bash "$REPO_ROOT/hooks/run-hook.cmd" session-start-codex`) with the compact payload.
